lead: White-box testing designs test cases by looking inside the code. The tester draws the control flow graph, counts its independent paths, and chooses inputs that make each path run. This finds unreachable code, wrong conditions and missing branches that black-box tests can miss. It is used at unit level, on safety-critical modules, and wherever coverage must be measured. The main method here is basis path testing; control structure testing adds condition, data flow and loop checks.
prereq: You need Chapter 4.1 for test cases, and basic programming control structures such as if, while and switch.

sections.h3: From code to a control flow graph

blocks.text: White-box testing is also called structural, glass-box or clear-box testing. The tester reads the source code and designs tests from its control flow. This differs from black-box testing, which uses only the specification.

A control flow graph (CFG) is a directed graph. A node is a statement or a block of statements that always execute together. An edge is a transfer of control from one node to another. The entry node is where execution starts; the exit node is where it stops. A decision node has two or more outgoing edges, one per outcome.
Coverage measures how much of the CFG the tests touch.

items: Statement coverage: every node runs at least once.
Branch or decision coverage: every edge out of every decision node runs at least once.
Condition coverage: each basic condition inside a compound decision takes both true and false.
Path coverage: every path from entry to exit runs. Loops can make this infinite, so full path coverage is rarely possible.

blocks.text: Statement coverage can reach 100 percent while a false branch is never taken. Branch coverage is stronger, but it still does not prove that every part of a compound condition was tested.

sections.h3: Cyclomatic complexity and a basis set

blocks.text: Cyclomatic complexity V(G) measures the number of independent paths through a CFG.

blocks.where: E is the number of edges; N is the number of nodes; P is the number of connected components, usually 1, so 2P is usually 2.

blocks.text: V(G) is the size of a basis set, not the total path count. A basis is a small set of paths from which every other path can be built by adding or removing loop iterations. A loop can give infinitely many paths, but V(G) stays finite.

items: Draw the CFG and number its nodes and edges.
Count E, N and P, then compute V(G).
Choose one baseline path from entry to exit.
Add one new edge at a time until you have V(G) paths; each new path must be independent.
Choose an input that forces each path to run.

blocks.text: For a structured program with one connected component, V(G) also equals the number of binary decisions plus one. Three independent paths means three tests in the basis set.
Control structure testing widens white-box testing beyond basis paths. It checks the internal structure of decisions, data and loops.

items: Condition testing: test each basic condition and each AND/OR combination. Watch short-circuit evaluation: in a && b, b is not evaluated when a is false.

Data flow testing: follow each variable from its definition to its uses. A define-use pair is a place where a variable is set and a later place where it is read. Undefined or dead values show up here.

Loop testing: for a loop that can run 0 to n times, test skip (0), once, twice, a typical value, n−1, n, and n+1 if the code allows it. For nested loops, test the inner loop with the outer at minimum and maximum.

blocks.text: A few advanced syllabi add symbolic execution, which runs code with symbol values, and model checking, which exhaustively checks a state model. Both are beyond this chapter.

figure.caption: Control flow graph for the worked example. Node 2 tests n > 0 and node 6 tests s > 10; the three independent paths differ at these two decisions.

spec.aria: A control flow graph with eight nodes: read n, test n > 0, two assignment branches, test s > 10, print large, print small, and end.

examples.question: A module runs: read n; if n > 0 then s = n + 1 else s = −n; if s > 10 then print 'large' else print 'small'. (a) Draw its CFG and count nodes and edges. (b) Compute V(G). (c) List three basis paths and give one input for each.
steps: Nodes: 1 read n; 2 decision n > 0; 3 s = n + 1; 5 s = −n; 6 decision s > 10; 7 print large; 9 print small; 10 end. The node numbers skip 4 and 8; only these eight nodes exist, so N = 8.
The graph is one connected component, so P = 1. V(G) = 9 − 8 + 2 × 1 = 3.
Baseline path 1-2-3-6-7-10. Input n = 12: n > 0 is true, s = 13, s > 10 is true, output is large.
Path 1-2-5-6-9-10. Input n = −5: n > 0 is false, s = 5, s > 10 is false, output is small.
Path 1-2-3-6-9-10. Input n = 5: n > 0 is true, s = 6, s > 10 is false, output is small.
examples.answer: V(G) = 3 independent paths; the three inputs are n = 12, n = −5 and n = 5.
examples.check:
E = 9
N = 8
P = 1
V = E - N + 2 * P
print(E)
print(N)
print(P)
print(V)

traps: V(G) is the size of a basis set, not the total number of paths. A loop can give infinite paths while V(G) stays small.
Forgetting the +2P term, or using E − N + 1 for a single component. The standard formula gives E − N + 2 when P = 1.
100 percent statement coverage can still miss a false branch; it does not guarantee branch coverage.

100 percent branch coverage does not guarantee condition coverage. For if (a > 0 && b < 5), the tests a = 5, b = 3 (true) and a = −1, b = 3 (false, short-circuited on a) give both branch outcomes, yet b < 5 is true in both tests, so it never takes the value false.

quiz.q: Define a control flow graph. What are its nodes and edges?
quiz.a: A directed graph of a program's control flow. A node is a statement or a block that always runs together; an edge is a transfer of control between nodes.

quiz.q: Write the formula for V(G) and define each term.
quiz.a: V(G) = E − N + 2P. E = number of edges, N = number of nodes, P = number of connected components, usually 1.

quiz.q: Why is V(G) not the total number of paths in a program?
quiz.a: V(G) is the number of independent paths in a basis. A loop can create infinitely many paths by repeating it, but the basis still has only V(G) paths.

quiz.q: A CFG has E = 13, N = 10 and P = 1. Compute V(G).
A decision is if (x > 0 && y < 10). Give tests for branch coverage and say whether they give condition coverage.
quiz.a: Branch coverage needs one true and one false outcome of the whole decision: x = 5, y = 5 gives true; x = −1, y = 5 gives false (short-circuit: y is not evaluated). These do not give condition coverage, because y < 10 is true in both tests and never takes false. Condition coverage needs both values of x > 0 and both values of y < 10, so four combinations (for example x = 5, y = 5; x = 5, y = 15; x = −1, y = 5; x = −1, y = 15).

quiz.q: A loop runs 0 to 100 times. List the loop tests for control structure testing.
quiz.a: Skip (0), once (1), twice (2), a typical value, 99, 100, and 101 if the code allows it or if the boundary must be rejected.

quiz.q: State one difference between statement coverage and branch coverage.
quiz.a: Statement coverage runs every node once. Branch coverage runs every edge out of every decision once, so it also checks both outcomes of each decision.

quiz.q: A module has V(G) = 4. A tester runs four paths but one path is not independent. Does this satisfy basis path testing? Explain.
quiz.a: No. A basis needs V(G) independent paths. If one path adds no new edge, the set covers fewer than four independent paths and some basis path is still untested.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry tools such as coverage analysers instrument the code and report statement and branch percentages after every test run. Search next for 'MC/DC coverage' (modified condition/decision coverage), which aviation and automotive safety standards use for compound decisions. Data flow testing tools track define-use pairs automatically. Model checking is used in chip design and in safety-critical protocols where exhaustive state exploration is affordable.
